title: Gold, trade, crops, herds
hookLine: zakat on cash and gold, trade goods, harvests and livestock, each with its rule

lines: A FARMER, A BOX OF GOLD.
cards: Four neighbors in an old market town. A shepherd, with a flock on the hills. A shopkeeper, with shelves of cloth waiting to be sold.
A farmer, with a field of wheat turning gold. And a woman with gold coins saved in a box under the bed. Each might owe zakat by the end of the year.
But you can't take a fortieth of a sheep, and you can't wait a year on a harvest that will rot. So zakat doesn't treat wealth as one heap. It sorts it, starting with the one that shines.

teach.b: First, gold and silver, and the money that now stands in for them. The Qur'an speaks hard words in surah nine about those who hoard gold and silver and don't spend it in the way of Allah.
Wealth kept still, in a box, is wealth zakat plainly reaches: one fortieth, once a year, above the line. Modern scholars put cash and bank savings here too.
Gold jewelry worn by a woman is where the schools of law differ: the Hanafi school counts it, and other schools, in general, don't count jewelry kept for wearing. Second, trade.
A report in the Sunan of Abu Dawud says the Prophet ﷺ commanded that charity be paid on what is prepared for sale.
So the shopkeeper's shelves count, valued at the zakat date as if they were money; scholars don't count the shelves themselves, the shop, the scales.
Third, crops. The Qur'an tells farmers to give the due on the day of the harvest. No waiting a year, and a different share; tomorrow is that day.
In Sahih al-Bukhari, Abu Bakr's letter of zakat sets out shares for camels and sheep, counted by heads, so a shepherd gives animals, not fractions. And what isn't counted?

A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says no charity is due from a Muslim on his horse or his slave, the things a person kept for his own use. Scholars take from it that your home, your car and your clothes are not zakat wealth.
Underneath all four: zakat looks at wealth that sits or wealth that grows, and leaves alone what you live with.

how: Muslims add up their zakatable wealth by category, cash and gold, trade stock, crops, livestock, and follow their school of law on questions such as worn jewelry, leaving out the home, car and personal belongings.

o: the only kind of wealth that zakat is ever paid on
jewelry, which every school counts the same way
the first of four kinds of zakat wealth, with money beside it

games.q: four kinds of wealth — tap the pairs.

s: zakat treats all wealth as one heap
it sorts wealth: gold and money, trade goods, crops and herds, each with its rule.
the shop and its scales are counted like the goods on the shelves
what's counted is what is prepared for sale, not the tools of the shop.
the schools of law differ on gold jewelry kept for wearing
the Hanafi school counts it; other schools, in general, don't.

games.q: you're the shepherd, and your zakat date arrives. how does Abu Bakr's letter have you give?
o: a fortieth of each sheep's value in coins.
animals, by the number of heads.
games.why: the letter sets shares counted by heads, so a shepherd gives animals, not fractions.

practice: Pick the kind of wealth closest to your life, money in a bank, things you sell, something you grow, animals you keep, and turn it over in your mind: is it still or moving, lived with or waiting to be used?
Then hold one thing that's just for living, a coat or a bike, and notice the difference.

wordCard.voice: Gold. The first of four kinds of zakat wealth, with silver and money; then trade goods, crops and herds, each with its own rule. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: gold, the first kind of zakat wealth.

carryVoice: Your line: each wealth has its share. Coins, shelves, fields and flocks, each counted its own way. Tomorrow: the harvest's tenth.
